text.en: Raju's village had a meeting about a new well. "Who decides these things?" he asked.

Local self-government means people manage local matters through elected bodies. In villages it is the Panchayat Raj, with the gram panchayat at the village level, panchayat union at the block and district panchayat above them. In towns we have municipalities and corporations.
The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments of 1992 gave these bodies constitutional status. Seats are reserved for women and for Scheduled Castes and Tribes, and elections are held every five years.
Local bodies look after water supply, roads, street lights, sanitation and schools. The gram sabha, the meeting of all adult villagers, lets people take part directly.

Local self-government means villagers and town residents elect their own neighbours to manage street lights, drinking water, village roads, drainage and primary health centres.

Local governance has deep roots in India. In Tamil Nadu, the tenth-century Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka Chola I describe how village sabhas elected committees via the Kudavolai palm-leaf ballot.
During British rule, Lord Ripon's Resolution of 1882 promoted elected municipal and rural boards, earning him the title 'Father of Local Self-Government in India'.
After independence, Mahatma Gandhi championed Gram Swaraj—self-reliant village republics—and Article 40 directed states to organise Village Panchayats.
In 1957, the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj structure, which was first inaugurated in Nagaur, Rajasthan in 1959.
Later, the Ashok Mehta Committee of 1977 suggested a two-tier system, and finally Parliament passed the landmark 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts in 1992.
The 73rd Amendment gave constitutional status to rural Panchayati Raj institutions and added the Eleventh Schedule listing twenty-nine rural development subjects.
At the foundation of every village stands the Gram Sabha—a meeting of all adult registered voters in the village—which approves budgets, audits works and questions elected leaders.

board.text: Gram Sabha: all adult voters in the village

text.en: In Tamil Nadu, Gram Sabha meetings are held regularly on key dates such as Republic Day, Labour Day, Independence Day and Gandhi Jayanti.

board.text: Regular Gram Sabha meetings in TN

text.en: Above the Gram Sabha sit the three tiers of Panchayati Raj: the Village Panchayat at the village level, the Panchayat Union (Block Samiti) at the block level, and the District Panchayat (Zila Parishad) at the district level.
Village Panchayats handle drinking water, street lighting, village roads, sanitation, rainwater harvesting and maintaining local libraries and parks.

Now look at urban local bodies strengthened by the 74th Amendment (Twelfth Schedule, eighteen subjects): Town Panchayats for transitional towns, Municipalities for medium towns, and Municipal Corporations for big cities.
Chennai's Corporation, founded in 1688, is the oldest Municipal Corporation in India! Today Tamil Nadu has twenty-one Municipal Corporations including Chennai, Madurai, Coimbatore, Trichy and Salem.
A Municipal Corporation is headed by an elected Mayor and assisted by a government-appointed Municipal Commissioner who executes council decisions.
Both rural and urban local elections are held every five years by an independent State Election Commission, and a State Finance Commission recommends how state taxes are shared with local bodies.

A transformative feature of the 73rd and 74th Amendments is mandatory reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and at least one-third for women—which Tamil Nadu raised to fifty percent!

board.text: 50% women's reservation in TN local bodies

text.en: Local bodies raise funds through property tax, water charges, trade licences, market fees and grants from State and Union governments.

board.text: Local revenue: property tax, fees & grants

text.en: Why is local self-government called the cradle of democracy? Because citizens learn leadership, budgeting and public service right in their own neighbourhood.
Common challenges include shortage of independent funds, irregular Gram Sabha attendance, and delays in devolving staff and powers from state departments.
Digital tools like e-GramSwaraj and online property-tax portals now make local budgets and public works far more transparent to citizens.
In Tamil Nadu, the Tamil Nadu Panchayats Act of 1994 brought state law in line with the 73rd Amendment, strengthening grassroots participation across all districts.

To identify the right local body for any place, check its population and setting: village -> Village Panchayat; small town -> Town Panchayat; medium town -> Municipality; large city -> Municipal Corporation.
Active participation in Gram Sabhas and ward meetings turns every citizen into a partner in building cleaner, safer and fairer communities.

board.text: Grassroots action builds stronger towns & villages

problem.en: A village wants a new overhead drinking-water tank and repaired street lights. Which local institution should citizens raise this at, and how is it funded?

text.en: Identify the right grassroots forum.

why.en: Villagers should place the request before the Gram Sabha, which reviews village needs and approves Village Panchayat plans.

text.en: Identify the executing tier.

why.en: The elected Village Panchayat prepares the estimate and carries out drinking-water and street-lighting works.

text.en: Identify the funding sources.

why.en: Funds come from local house/property taxes, State Finance Commission grants and rural development schemes.
